name: Latha
definition: Latha is a composite portrait of a woman balancing seasonal factory work with household responsibilities in Puttur taluk, where cashew processing remains a major employer for women from the Billava and other coastal communities. She represents the thousands of women whose daily economic contribution comes from low-wage seasonal work in Dakshina Kannada's cashew industry, while managing children's schooling and household duties in a district known paradoxically for both high literacy and persistent dropout concerns.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Latha works six months of the year in a cashew processing unit near Puttur town, peeling and grading kernels under a piece-rate system that pays roughly Rs 350-450 per day depending on the daily quota she meets. The work is seated but repetitive, her fingers stained dark from the cashew-nut shell liquid, and the unit shuts down during the off-season when raw nuts run out, leaving her without wages for three to four months. She leaves home by seven-thirty in the morning, takes the Shakti bus to the unit, works until five, and returns by six-thirty, her back aching from the long hours hunched over the sorting table. The household depends on her earnings during the season to cover school fees, medical expenses and groceries, since her husband's income as a small-scale arecanut trader fluctuates with harvest cycles and market prices. During the off-season she takes up casual agricultural labour during the arecanut and coconut harvest, earning Rs 300-350 per day for climbing and plucking, work that is harder physically but necessary to keep some income flowing into the household.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Latha lives with her husband, two children and her mother-in-law in a small tiled house on the edge of Puttur town, a household arrangement common in her community where the eldest son remains with his parents. Her daughter is fourteen and studying in Class 9 at the government high school in Puttur, while her son is eleven and in Class 6 at the same school. Her husband manages a small arecanut trading business, buying from local farmers and selling to agents connected to CAMPCO, but his income is seasonal and uncertain, particularly when Yellow Leaf Disease affects the crop and prices drop. Her mother-in-law, now in her sixties, manages the cooking and household chores when Latha is at work, a division of labour that allows Latha to continue factory employment but also means she must defer to the older woman's opinions on spending and child-rearing. The family follows Billava community customs, with ties to the local Bhuta shrine and participation in the Koti-Chennaya rituals during the annual festival, though Latha herself has little time for extended social or ritual obligations during the cashew season.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Latha studied only until Class 7 before her parents pulled her out to work, a common pattern in her generation, though she now insists her daughter must finish at least SSLC. Her daughter attends the government Kannada-medium high school in Puttur, where fees are minimal but the family spends around Rs 800-1,000 per month on books, uniform, bus fare for college visits and tuition for mathematics and science, subjects the girl finds difficult. Latha's hope is that her daughter will finish Class 10, perhaps even PU college, and find work in a bank or government office rather than the cashew unit, though private English-medium schools in Puttur remain out of reach financially and her mother-in-law questions the need for more schooling once a girl reaches marriage age. Her son studies in the same school and performs better academically, and Latha dreams he might reach degree level and escape manual labour altogether, though she worries about affording PU college fees if he makes it that far. During the off-season when Latha herself is not working, she can supervise homework more closely, but during the cashew season her mother-in-law takes over and is less vigilant, so the children's performance slips slightly each year between October and March.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Latha suffers from chronic lower-back pain and numbness in her fingers from years of cashew peeling, conditions common among processing-unit women but rarely treated beyond occasional painkillers bought from the local pharmacy. The household is enrolled in Ayushman Bharat-Arogya Karnataka, and when her mother-in-law needed cataract surgery two years ago they travelled to Father Muller's Hospital in Mangaluru, paying only a small co-payment under the scheme, though the travel and food costs added up. Her daughter has had recurrent respiratory infections, which Latha attributes to the damp climate and the crowded classroom, and she worries about the cost of continued doctor visits if the problem becomes serious, since the nearest primary health centre is under-staffed and referrals mean losing a full day's work for travel to Mangaluru. Her husband smokes beedis and has begun coughing frequently, a source of tension in the household since Latha fears he will need expensive treatment they cannot afford and he refuses to visit a doctor. The processing unit provides no health insurance, no sick leave and no compensation for work-related injuries, so when Latha once cut her hand badly on a broken shell she lost three days' wages while it healed and paid for the bandages herself. She has heard of Endosulfan-affected families in Puttur taluk receiving pensions, though none in her immediate circle, and worries vaguely about the long-term health effects of cashew-shell chemicals but has no alternative source of income.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Latha's family belongs to the Billava community, historically associated with toddy-tapping but now widely engaged in trade, labour and small-scale farming across Dakshina Kannada. The community is politically organised and owns a prominent role in local Bhuta Kola rituals, particularly those invoking Koti and Chennaya, the twin heroes of the Billava epic; Latha's husband's family has ties to the Bhuta shrine near their house and contributes money and labour during the annual night-long Kola ceremony. Latha herself feels pride in the community's rising social and economic status, though she is aware that Bunt and Brahmin families in Puttur still command more land and educational capital. She speaks Tulu at home, Kannada at the processing unit and in government offices, and her children are more comfortable in Kannada than Tulu, a shift she accepts as inevitable given the school and media environment. The family has social ties within the Billava neighbourhood, particularly among other cashew-unit women who travel together on the Shakti bus and share information about work, wages and children's schooling, a network that offers both material support and collective grievance when the unit management delays wages or cuts rates. Latha attends temple festivals and the annual Marikamba Jatre when time and money allow, though her mother-in-law is more observant and insists on household rituals that Latha finds time-consuming.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Latha has a ration card, an Aadhaar card and a bank account opened under a local self-help group linked to SKDRDP, though she rarely uses the account since her daily wages are paid in cash and deposited at home. The family received a small loan from the self-help group three years ago to repair the house roof, which they repaid in monthly instalments, and Latha values the group's savings discipline even though the weekly meetings are hard to attend during the cashew season. Her daughter's school fees are partly covered by scholarships for SC/ST and OBC students, which arrive late and irregularly, forcing the family to borrow from relatives at the start of each academic year. She has never attended a gram panchayat meeting or spoken to an elected representative directly, feeling that such spaces are for men and for people with more education and confidence. The Shakti free-bus scheme has made a tangible difference to her daily travel costs, saving the household roughly Rs 1,500-2,000 per month, money she now redirects toward groceries and her daughter's tuition fees. She has heard of Ayushman Bharat and uses it when necessary, but finds the referral process complicated and the private hospitals intimidating.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: She blames the processing-unit owners for low wages and exploitative piece-rates, the school for charging hidden fees despite being government-run, and her husband for not earning a stable income, though she knows his arecanut-trading income depends on forces beyond his control, particularly crop disease and price crashes. She dreams her son might reach degree level and find a salaried office job in Mangaluru or Bengaluru, while her daughter should at least finish SSLC before marriage, giving her some independence and respect. Latha resents that private English-medium schools are only for the well-off, leaving her children in Kannada-medium schools where, she fears, the teaching is less rigorous and the future prospects narrower. She worries about her own health and what will happen to the household if she can no longer work, since there is no pension, no savings and no safety net beyond family.
